```{r}
#| include: false
require(mosaic)
require(gridExtra)
```

# CLT and $\bar X$

We know $\bar X$ has a normal sampling
distribution if we draw iid samples from a normal
population.  The CLT indicates this is true, when
the sample size $n$ is large enough, even when
drawing from non-normal populations.

### Drawing from a uniform distribution

Let us draw samples of size 10 from Unif$(2,6)$.
```{r}
#| fig-height: 2
#| fig-width: 6
#| warning: false
manyXbars = replicate(10000, mean(~ runif(10,2,6)))
p1 = gf_qq(~manyXbars)
p2 = gf_dhistogram(~manyXbars) |> gf_dist("norm", mean=4, sd=sqrt(4/30), color="red")
grid.arrange(p1, p2, ncol=2)
```

### Drawing from an exponential distribution

Let us draw samples of size 10 from Exp$(8)$.
```{r}
#| fig-height: 2
#| fig-width: 6
#| warning: false
n=30
manyXbars = replicate(10000, mean(~ rexp(n,8)))
p1 = gf_qq(~manyXbars)
p2 = gf_dhistogram(~manyXbars) |> gf_dist("norm", mean=1/8, sd=1/(8*sqrt(n)), color="red")
grid.arrange(p1, p2, ncol=2)
```

A long-accepted rule has been that $n\ge 30$
is sufficiently large to conclude $\bar X$
has a normal distribution, though examples
like this one call into question whether
this is true when drawing from a highly
skewed population.

# CLT and $\hat p$

### iid draws from Binom$(1,\pi)$

First, I drawn $n=10$ times and calculate the
mean, which corresponds to the sample proportion
$\hat p$:
```{r}
#| fig-height: 2
#| fig-width: 6
#| warning: false
n=10
manyPhats = replicate(100000, mean(~rbinom(n, 1, 0.3)))
p1 = gf_histogram(~manyPhats, binwidth=0.1, color="black")
p2 = gf_qq(~manyPhats)
grid.arrange(p1,p2,ncol=2)
```

The sampling distribution of $\hat p$ does not
appear to be especially normal.
Note that I used the value $\pi=0.3$, and so
$$ n\pi = 3 \qquad\mbox{and}\qquad n(1-\pi) = 7. $$

If I replace the `mean()` command by `sum()` in
the code above, I'll be producing a simulated
sampling distribution of $X$, the *count* (instead
of the *proportion*) of successes.  The last run
illustrates the sampling distribution does *not*
need to be normal.  Nevertheless, this rule
regarding the interplay between sample size
and $\pi$, namely
$$ n\pi \ge 10 \qquad\mbox{and}\qquad
  n(1-\pi)\ge 10, $$ 
is widely accepted as sufficient to consider
the sampling distributions approximately normal
for both $\hat p$ and $X\sim$ Binom$(n,\pi)$:

 * $\hat p = \frac{1}{n}(X_1 + \cdots + X_n)$
   has an approximate normal distribution
   Norm$(\pi, \sqrt{\frac{\pi(1-pi)}{n}})$, and
 * $X = n\hat p$ is approximately distributed as
   Norm$(n\pi, \sqrt{n\pi(1-pi)})$,
   
when $n\pi \ge 10$ and $n(1-\pi)\ge 10$, assuming
that the $X_i\sim$ Binom$(1,\pi)$ are independent.

# Continuity correction

The rule, $n\pi\ge 10$ and $n(1-\pi)\ge 10$ is
met when $n=50$ and $\pi=0.3$.  This should, by
the statements above, make it viable to obtain
probabilities for $X\sim$ Binom$(50,0.3)$ from
`pnorm()` where the normal distribution
Norm$(50,0.3)$ is assumed.  See the figure,
which overlays the two distributions.

```{r}
#| fig-height: 2.5
#| warning: false
gf_dist("binom", size=50, prob=0.3, kind="histogram", binwidth=1, color="black",
        fill="#6B8ED6") |>
  gf_dist("norm", mean=15, sd=sqrt(15*.7), color="red")
```

Note that the binomial cdf function for values
up to and including 10 disagrees with the normal
cdf function.
```{r}
pbinom(10,50,.3)
pnorm(10, 15, sqrt(50*.3*.7))
```
The picture, itself, suggests that replacing the
discrete probabilities (blue rectangles) with
continuous ones (area under the red curve) will
lead to errors, much as calculus students learn
to have discrepancies between true areas under
curves and the approximations obtained using
Riemann sums.  That we might undertake some sort
of *continuity correction* seems natural.

Just imagine, for the moment, computing the
probability of the value $X=10$.  An error-free
way, using the binomial cdf, is
```{r}
pbinom(10,50,0.3) - pbinom(9,50,0.3)
```
Attempting to approximate this value using the
normal cdf, you can see that
```{r}
#| eval: false
pnorm(10, 15, sqrt(50*0.3*0.7))- pnorm(10, 15, sqrt(50*0.3*0.7))
```
is a feeble effort giving zero, and
```{r}
#| eval: false
pnorm(10, 15, sqrt(50*0.3*0.7))- pnorm(9, 15, sqrt(50*0.3*0.7))
```
though an improvement, seems to be the wrong
width-one section of area under the red curve.
It would be better to get the area between $9.5$
and $10.5$.  Similarly, `pbinom(10, 50, 0.3)`
should be better-approximated using the normal
probability up to 10.5 instead of 10:
```{r}
pnorm(10.5, 15, sqrt(50*0.3*0.7))
```
Indeed, $0.082$ is closer to $0.079$ than
$0.061$.
